overview.text: A caldera is a large, basin-shaped volcanic depression. In a common formation process, an eruption expels or withdraws magma from a shallow underground reservoir; the loss of support allows the overlying ground to subside or collapse. Calderas can form at the summit of an existing volcano or as much larger volcanic basins. Their sunken floors may collect rain and snow to form lakes, and later eruptions can build new volcanic features inside them. Crater Lake occupies the caldera left by Mount Mazama, while Yellowstone’s plateau contains several calderas. These landscapes preserve evidence of major eruptions and the changing structure of volcanoes.

key_facts.text: Calderas commonly form when magma is withdrawn or erupted from a shallow reservoir, removing support from the overlying rock and allowing the ground to collapse.
The magma chamber does not have to empty completely: the National Park Service describes caldera formation after a chamber is partially emptied during a large eruption.
Mount Mazama’s eruption about 7,700 years ago formed a caldera about 8–10 km across and 1.2 km deep.
Rain and snow partly filled the Crater Lake caldera over several hundred years; later eruptions formed Wizard Island and underwater volcanic features.
The Yellowstone Plateau contains three separate calderas, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
